paper.title: Consistency of Neural Causal Partial Identification
paper.authors: Jiyuan Tan, Jose Blanchet, Vasilis Syrgkanis
paper.html:
Abstract

Recent progress in Neural Causal Models (NCMs) showcased how identification and partial identification of causal effects can be automatically carried out via training of neural generative models that respect the constraints encoded in a given causal graph [51; 3]. However, formal consistency of these methods has only been proven for the case of discrete variables or only for linear causal models. In this work, we prove the consistency of partial identification via NCMs in a general setting with both continuous and categorical variables. Further, our results highlight the impact of the design of the underlying neural network architecture in terms of depth and connectivity as well as the importance of applying Lipschitz regularization in the training phase. In particular, we provide a counterexample showing that without Lipschitz regularization this method may not be asymptotically consistent. Our results are enabled by new results on the approximability of Structural Causal Models (SCMs) via neural generative models, together with an analysis of the sample complexity of the resulting architectures and how that translates into an error in the constrained optimization problem that defines the partial identification bounds.

1 Introduction

Identifying causal quantities from observational data is an important problem in causal inference which has wide applications in economics [1], social science [20], health care [34; 18], and recommendation systems [9]. One common approach is to transform causal quantities into statistical quantities using the ID algorithm [48] and deploy general purpose methods to estimate the statistical quantity. However, in the presence of unobserved confounding, typically the causal quantity of interest will not be point-identified by observational data, unless special mechanisms are present in the data generating process (e.g. instruments, unconfounded mediators, proxy controls). In the presence of unobserved confounding, the ID algorithm will typically fail to return a statistical quantity and declare the causal quantity as non-identifiable.
One remedy to this problem, which we focus on in this paper, is partial identification, which aims to give informative bounds for causal quantities based on the available data. At a high level, partial identification bounds can be defined as follows: find the maximum and the minimum value that a target causal quantity can take, among all Structural Causal Models (SCMs) that give rise to the same observed data distribution and respect the given causal graph (as well as any other structural constraints that one is willing to impose). Note that in the presence of unobserved confounding, there will typically exist many structural mechanisms that could give rise to the same observational distribution but have vastly different counterfactual distributions. Hence, partial identification can be formulated as solving a max and a min optimization problem [3]
M∈Cmax​\M∈Cmin​subject to​ θ(M), PM(V)=PM∗(V),andGM​=GM∗​,​(1.1)​
where θ(M) is the causal quantity of interest, M∗ is the true model, V is the set of observed nodes, PM(V) is the distribution of V in SCM M, C is a collection of causal models and GM​ is the causal graph of M (see 2 for formal definitions). Two recent lines of work explore the optimization approach to partial identification. The first line deals with discrete Structure Causal Models (SCMs), where all observed variables are finitely supported. In this case, (1.1) becomes a Linear Programming (LP) or polynomial programming problem and tight bounds can be obtained [37; 4; 5; 27; 44; 45; 40; 8; 53; 55; 14]. The second line of work focuses on continuous models and explores ways of solving (1.1) in continuous settings using various techniques [24; 32; 29; 38; 3; 41].
Recently, Xia et al. [50] formalized the connection between SCMs and generative models (see also [33] for an earlier version of a special case of this connection). This work showcased that SCMs can be interpreted as neural generative models, namely Neural Causal Models (NCMs), that follow a particular architecture that respects the constraints encoded in a given causal graph. Hence, counterfactual quantities of SCMs can be learned by optimizing over the parameters of the underlying generative models. However, there could be multiple models that lead to the same observed data distribution, albeit have different counterfactual distributions. Xia et al. [50] first analyze the approximation power of NCMs for discrete SCMs and employ the max/min approach to verify the identifiability of causal quantities, without the need to employ the ID algorithm. Balazadeh et al. [3] and Hui et al. [30], extend the method in [50] and re-purpose it to perform partial identification by solving the min and max problem in the partial identification formulation over neural causal models.
However, for SCMs with general random variables and functional relationships, the approximation error and consistency of this optimization-based approach to partial identification via NCMs has not been established. In particular, two problems remain open. First, given an arbitrary SCM, it is not yet known if we can find an NCM that produces approximately the same intervention distribution as the original one. Although Xia et al.[50] show it is possible to represent any discrete SCM by an NCM, their construction highly relies on the discrete assumption and cannot be directly generalized to the general case. Moreover, Xia et al. [50] use step functions as the activation function in their construction, which may create difficulties in the training process since step functions are discontinuous with a zero gradient almost everywhere.
Second, since we only have access to n samples from the true distribution, PM(V), we need to replace the constraints in (1.1) with their empirical version that uses the empirical distribution of samples PnM∗​(V) in place of the population distribution and looks for NCMs, whose implied distribution lies within a small distance from the empirical distribution. Moreover, even the NCM distribution is typically only accessible through sampling, hence we will need to generate mn​ samples from the NCM and use the empirical distribution of the mn​ samples from the NCM in place of the true distribution implied by the NCM. Thus, in practice, we will use a constraint of the form d(PnM∗​(V),Pmn​M​(V))⩽αn​, where d is some notion of distribution distance and αn​ accounts for the sampling error. It is not clear that this approach is consistent, converges to the correct partial identification bounds, when the sample size n grows to infinity. Balazadeh et al. [3] only show the consistency of this approach for linear SCMs. Consistency results concerning more general SCMs is still lacking in the neural causal literature.
In this paper, we establish representation and consistency results for general SCMs. Our contributions are summarized as follows.
  • We show that under suitable regularity assumptions, given any Lipschitz SCM, we can approximate it using an NCM such that the Wasserstein distance between any interventional distribution of the NCM and the original SCM is small. Each random variable of the SCM is allowed to be continuous or categorical. We specify two architectures of the Neural Networks (NNs) that can be trained using common gradient-based optimization algorithms (Theorem 3.6 and Corollary 3.7).
  • To construct the NCM approximation, we develop a novel representation theorem of probability measures (Proposition B.2) that may be of independent interest. Proposition B.2 implies that under certain assumptions, probability distributions supported on the unit cube can be simulated by pushing forward a multivariate uniform distribution.
  • We discover the importance of Lipschitz regularization by constructing a counterexample where the neural causal approach is not consistent without regularization (Proposition 4.1).
  • Using Lipschitz regularization, we prove the consistency of the neural causal approach (Theorem 4.2).
Related Work There exists a rich literature on partial identification of average treatment effects (ATE) [37; 4; 5; 27; 44; 45; 40; 8; 53; 55; 14; 7; 39; 26].
Balke and Pearl [4; 5] first give an algorithm to calculate bounds on the ATE in the Instrumental Variable (IV) setting. They show that regardless of the exact distribution of the latent variables, it is sufficient to consider discrete latent variables as long as all endogenous variables are finitely supported. Moreover, they discover that (1.1) is an LP problem with a closed-form solution. This LP-based technique was generalized to several special classes of SCMs [44; 8; 27; 46].
For general discrete SCMs, [14; 55; 54] consider transforming the problem (1.1) into a polynomial programming problem. Xia et al. [50] discover the connection between generative models and SCMs. They show that NCMs are expressive enough to approximate discrete SCMs. By setting C in problem (1.1) to be the collection of NCMs, they apply NCMs for identification and estimation.
For causal models with continuous random variables, the constraints in (1.1) become integral equations, which makes the problem more difficult. One approach is to discretize the constraints. [24] uses stochastic process representation of the causal model in the continuous IV setting and transforms the problem into a semi-infinite program. [32] relaxes the constraints to finite moment equations and solves the problem by the Augmented Lagrangian Method (ALM). The other approach is to use generative models to approximate the observational distribution and use some metric to measure the distance between distributions. [33] first propose to use GAN to generate images. Later, [29] uses Wasserstein distance in the constraint and transforms the optimization problem into a min and max problem. Similarly, [3] solves the optimization problem using Sinkhorn distance to avoid instability during training. They propose to estimate the Average Treatment Derivative (ATD) and use ATD to obtain a bound on the ATE. They also prove the consistency of the proposed estimator for linear SCMs. [41] uses a linear combination of basis functions to approximate response functions. [26] uses sieve to solve the resulting optimization problem in the IV setting. [19] proposes a neural network framework for sensitivity analysis under unobserved confounding.
Organization of this paper In 2, we introduce the notations and some basic concepts used throughout the paper. Next, in 3, we demonstrate how to construct an NCM so that they can approximate a given SCM arbitrarily well. Two kinds of architecture are given along with an approximation error analysis. In 4, we highlight the importance of Lipschitz regularization by giving a counterexample that is not consistent. Then, leveraging the previous approximation results, we are able to prove the consistency of this approach under regularization. Finally, we compare our method with the traditional polynomial programming method empirically in 5.

2 Preliminary

First, we introduce the definition of an SCM. Throughout the paper, we use bold symbols to represent sets of random variables.
Definition 2.1.
(Structural Causal Model) A Structural Causal Model (SCM) is a tuple M=(V,U,F,P(U),G0​), where V={Vi​}i=1nV​​ is the set of observed variables; U={Uj​}j=1nU​​ is the set of latent variables; P(U) is the distribution of latent variables; G0​ is an acyclic directed graph whose nodes are V. The values of each observed variable Vi​ are generated by
Vi​=fi​(Pa(Vi​),UVi​​),where Vi​∈/Pa(Vi​) and UVi​​⊂U,(2.1)
where F=(f1​,⋯,fnV​​), Pa(V) is the set of parents of V in graph G0​ and UVi​​ is the set of latent variables that affect Vi​. Vi​ takes either continuous values Rdi​ or categorical in [ni​]. We extend graph G0​ by adding bi-directed arrows between any Vi​,Vj​∈G0​ if there exists a correlated latent variable pair (Uk​,Ul​),Uk​∈UVi​​,Ul​∈UVj​​. We call the extended graph GM​ the causal graph of M.
When we write Pa(Vi​), we refer to the parents of Vi​ in the G0​. To connect with the literature, the causal graph we define is a kind of Acyclic Directed Mixed Graph (ADMG), which is often used to represent SCMs with unobserved variables [48]. Note that we allow one latent variable to enter several nodes, which differs from the common definition. We use nU​ and nV​ to denote the number of latent variables and observable variables. Let T⊂V be a set of treatment variables. The goal is to estimate causal quantities under a given intervention T=t. Formally, the structural equations of the intervened model are
​Ti​=ti​,∀Ti​∈T,Vi​(t)=fi​(Pa(Vi​),UVi​​),∀Vi​∈/T.​
We denote Vi​(t) to be the value of Vi​ under the intervention T=t and PM(V(t)) to be the distribution of V(t) in M. The notion of a C2 component [50] is defined as follows.
Definition 2.2 (C2-Component).
For a causal graph G, a subset C⊂V is C2-component if each pair Vi​,Vj​∈C is connected by a bi-directed arrow in G and C is maximal.
We provide a concrete example in A to explain all these notions. We will make the following standard assumption about the independence of latent variables. Note that since we allow latent variables to enter in multiple structural equations, this is more a notational convention and not an actual assumption. Also note that under this convention a bi-directed arrow essentially represents the existence of a common latent parental variable.
Assumption 2.3.
All the latent variables in U are independent.
To deal with categorical variables, we assume that latent variables that influence categorical variables contain two parts: the shared confounding that influences the propensity functions and the independent noise that generates categorical distributions.
Assumption 2.4.
The set of latent variables consists of two parts U={U1​,⋯,UnU​​}∪{GVi​​:Vi​ is categorical}. Precisely, if Vi​∈V is a categorical variable, the data generation process of Vi​ satisfies Vi​=argmaxk∈[ni​]​{gkVi​​+log(fi​(Pa(Vi​),UVi​​))k​}∼Categorical(fi​/∥fi​∥1​), where GVi​​=(g1Vi​​,⋯,gni​Vi​​) are i.i.d. standard Gumbel variables, UVi​​⊂{U1​,⋯,UnU​​}.
This convention is without loss of generality at this point, but will be useful when introducing Lispchitz restrictions on the structural equation functions. The Gumbel variables in the assumption can be replaced by any random variables that can generate categorical variables. It can be proven that all discrete SCMs satisfy this assumption. Note that we implicitly assume that all categorical variables Vi​ are supported on [ni​] for some ni​. It is straightforward to generalize all results to any finite support. Next, we introduce Neural Causal Models (NCMs).
Definition 2.5.
Original (Neural Causal Model) A Neural Causal Model (NCM) is a special kind of SCM where U={U1​,⋯,UnU​​}∪{GVi​​:Vi​ categorical}, all Ui​ are i.i.d. multivariate uniform variables, GVi​​ are i.i.d Gumblel variables and functions in (2.1) are Neural Networks (NNs).
Corrected
(Neural Causal Model) A Neural Causal Model (NCM) is a special kind of SCM where U={U1​,…,UnU​​}∪{GVi​​:Vi​ categorical}, the scalar coordinates of all the Ui​ are mutually independent with common Unif([0,1]) law, and Ui​ groups the indicated finite number diU​ of these coordinates, so that Ui​∼Unif([0,1]diU​).
All coordinates of the GVi​​ are independent standard Gumbel variables, independent of all uniform coordinates.
The continuous structural maps and the categorical propensity-weight maps fi​ in (2.1) are Neural Networks (NNs); categorical values are generated from these weights by the Gumbel argmax rule.
The weights are nonnegative and have strictly positive sum, with log0=−∞.
The definition of NCMs we use is slightly different from that in [51] because we need to deal with mixed variables in our models. In (1.1), we usually take C to be the set of all SCMs. However, it is difficult to search over all SCMs since (1.1) becomes an infinite-dimensional polynomial programming problem. As an alternative, we can search over all NCMs. One quantity of common interest in causal inference is the Average Treatment Effect (ATE).
Definition 2.6.
(Average Treatment Effect). For SCM M, the ATE at T=t with respect to T=t0​ is given by ATEM​(t)=Eu∼P(U)​[Y(t)−Y(t0​)].
Partial identification can be formulated as estimating the solution to the optimization problems (1.1) [3]. The max and min values F and F​ define the interval [F​,F] which is the smallest interval we can derive from the observed data without additional assumptions. In particular, if F=F​, then the causal quantity is point-identified.
Notations. We use ∥⋅∥,∥⋅∥∞​ for the 1-norm and ∞-norm and [n] for {1,⋯,n}. Bold letters represent sets of random variables. We let FL​(K1​,K2​) be the class of Lipschitz L-continuous functions f:K1​→K2​. We may omit the domain and use FL​ when the domain is clear from context. Let H(K1​,K2​) be the set of homeomorphisms from K1​ to K2​, i.e., injective and continuous maps in both directions. We define ϵ(F1​,F2​)=supf2​∈F2​​inff1​∈F1​​∥f2​−f1​∥ for function classes F1​,F2​. We use standard asymptotic notation O(⋅),Ω(⋅). Given a measure μ on Rd1​ and a measurable function f:Rd1​→Rd2​, the push-forward measure f#​μ is defined as f#​μ(B)=μ(f−1(B)) for all measurable sets B. We use P(X) to represent the distribution of random variable X. Let Δn​={(p1​,⋯,pn​):∑i=1n​pi​=1,pi​⩾0} be the probability simplex. We use Categorical(p),p∈Δn​ to represent categorical distribution with event probability p. We let W(⋅,⋅) be the Wasserstein-1 distance and Sλ​(μ,ν) be the Sinkhorn distance [12] with regularization parameter λ>0.

3 Approximation Error of Neural Causal Models

In this section, we study the expressive power of NCMs, which serves as a key ingredient in proving the consistency result. In particular, given an SCM M∗, we want to construct an NCM M^ such that the two causal models produce similar interventional results. Unlike in the discrete case [4; 50], latent distributions can be extremely complicated in general cases. The main challenge is how to design the structure of NCMs to ensure strong approximation power.
In the following, we first derive an upper bound on the Wasserstein distance between two causal models sharing the same causal graph. Using this result, we decompose the approximation error into two parts: the error caused by approximating structural functions via neural networks and the error of approximating the latent distributions. Then, we design different architectures for these two parts.
Decomposing the Approximation Error
First, we present a canonical representation of an SCM, which essentially states that we only need to consider the case where each latent variable Ui​ corresponds to a C2 component of G.
Definition 3.1 (Canonical representation).
A SCM M with causal graph G has canonical form if
  1. The set of latent variables consists of two sets,
    U={UC​:C is a C2-component of G}∪{GVi​​=(g1Vi​​,⋯,gni​Vi​​):Vi​ is categorical},
    where UC​ and gjVi​​ are independent and gjVi​​ are standard Gumbel variables.
  2. The structure equations have the form
    Vi​={fi​(Pa(Vi​),UVi​​),argmaxk∈[ni​]​{gkVi​​+log(fi​(Pa(Vi​),UVi​​))k​},​Vi​ is continuous,Vi​ is categorical,∥fi​∥1​=1,​(3.1)
    where UVi​​={UC​:Vi​∈C,C is a C2-component of G} and (x)k​ is the k-th coordinate of the vector x. We further assume that fi​ are normalized for categorical variables.
Given a function class F, the SCM class M(G,F,U) consists of all canonical SCM models with causal graph G such that fi​∈F,i∈[nV​].
Proposition B.1 in the appendix shows that any SCM satisfying Assumption 2.3,2.4 can be represented in this way and we provide an example in B.1 to illustrate how to obtain the canonical representation for a given SCM. Therefore, we restrict our attention to the class M(G,F,U). For two SCM classes M(G,F,U),M(G,F^,U^), we want to study how well we can represent the models in the first class by the second class. The Wasserstein distance between the intervention distributions is used to measure the quality of the approximation. To approximate the functions in the structural equations, we need to make the following regularity assumptions on the functions.
Assumption 3.2.
If Vi​ is continuous, fi​ in (3.1) are Lf​-Lipschitz continuous. If Vi​ is categorical, the propensity functions fi​(Pa(Vi​),UVi​​)≜P(Vi​=j∣Pa(Vi​),UVi​​),j∈[ni​] are Lf​-Lipschitz continuous. There exists a constant K>0 such that maxi∈[nV​],j∈[nU​]​{∥Vi​∥∞​,∥Uj​∥∞​}⩽K.
The following theorem summarizes our approximation error decomposition.
Theorem 3.3.
Given any SCM model M∈M(G,FL​,U), let the treatment variable set be T={Tk​}k=1nt​​ and suppose that Assumption 2.3, 2.4 and 3.2 hold for M with Lipschitz constant L, constant K.
Original For any intervention T=t and M^∈M(G,F^,U^) , we have
W(PM(V(t)),PM^(V^(t)))⩽CG​(L,K)(i=1∑nV​​∥fi​−f^​i​∥∞​+W(PM(U),PM^(U^))),(4)
where CG​(L,K) is a constant that only depends on L,K and the causal graph G and fi​,f^​i​ are structural functions of M and M^ respectively.
Corrected For any intervention T=t and M^∈M(G,F^,U^), we have
W(PM(V(t)),PM^(V^(t)))⩽CG​(L,K;{di​,ni​})(i=1∑nV​​∥fi​−f^​i​∥∞​+W(PM(U),PM^(U^))),
where CG​(L,K;{di​,ni​}) is a constant that only depends on L,K, the causal graph G, the continuous output dimensions di​, and the categorical cardinalities ni​, and fi​,f^​i​ are structural functions of M and M^ respectively.
Theorem 3.3 separates the approximation error into two parts, which motivates us to construct the NCM in the following way. First, we approximate the functions fi​ in (3.1) by NNs f^​i​. Then, we approximate the distribution of latent variables by pushing forward uniform and Gumbel variables using neural networks, i.e., U^Cj​​=g^​j​(ZCj​​), where {Cj​} are C2 components and ZCj​​ are multi-variate uniform and Gumbel random variables. The structural equations of the resulting approximated model M^ are
V^i​=⎩⎨⎧​f^​i​(Pa(V^i​),(g^​j​(ZCj​​))UCj​​∈UVi​​​),argmaxk∈[ni​]​{gk​+log(f^​i​(Pa(V^i​),(g^​j​(ZCj​​))UCj​​∈UVi​​​))k​},​Vi​ is continuous,Vi​ is categorical.​(3.3)
For the first part, we need to approximate Lipschitz continuous functions. For simplicity, we assume that the domain of the functions are uniform cubes. Similar arguments hold for any bounded cubes. We denote NNk1​,k2​​(W,L) to be the set of ReLu NNs with input dimension k1​, output dimension k2​, width W and depth L. It has been shown that ϵ(NNk1​,1​(2d1​+10,L0​),FL​([0,1]d1​,R))⩽O(L0−2/k1​​) [52], where ϵ(⋅,⋅) denotes the approximation error defined in 2. For a vector valued function, we can use a wider NN to approximate each coordinate and get a similar rate.
For the second part, we approximate each Ui​ individually by pushing forward i.i.d. multivariate uniform and Gumbel variables U^Ci​​=g^​i​(ZCi​​) since the latent variables are independent by Assumption 2.3. To do so, we examine under what assumptions on the measure P over Rn we can find a NN g^​ such that W(g^​#​λ,P) is small, where λ(⋅) is some reference measure.

3.1 Approximating Mixed Distributions by Neural Networks

In this subsection, we will extend the results in [43] to construct a neural network as the push-forward map. It turns out that to get a good approximation of the targeted distribution, the shape of the support is essential. We introduce the following two assumptions for our latent distribution.
Assumption 3.4 (Mixed Distribution).
The support of measure P has finite connected components C1​,C2​⋯CNC​​, i.e., supp(P)=⋃i=1NC​​Ci​, and each component Ci​ satisfies H([0,1]diC​,Ci​)∩FL​([0,1]diC​,Ci​)=∅ for some diC​⩾0. Recall that H(K1​,K2​) is the set of homeomorphisms from K1​ to K2​ defined at the end of 2.
Assumption 3.4 encompasses almost all natural distributions. For example, distributions supported on [0,1]d and closed balls, finitely supported distributions and mixtures of them all satisfy this assumption. Assumption 3.4 allows us to transform the support of the targeted distribution into unit cubes and the nice geometric properties of unit cubes facilitate our construction. The next assumption is slightly than Assumption 3.4, but we will show later that it can give us a better rate.
Assumption 3.5 (Lower Bound).
Suppose that P is supported on a compact set K⊂RD, there exists a constant Cf​>0, f∈H([0,1]d,K)∩FL​([0,1]d,K), such that for any measurable set B⊂[0,1]d, P(f(B))⩾Cf​λ(B).
Original Besides, if d>0, f#​P vanishes on the boundary ∂[0,1]d.
Corrected Besides, if d>0, (f−1)#​P vanishes on the boundary ∂[0,1]d.
Assumption 3.5 implies that dλ/d(f#−1​P) exists and is lowered bounded by a constant Cf​. We show in the appendix (Proposition B.2) that under Assumption 3.5, it is possible to simulate any distribution on the unit cubes with Hölder continuous curves and uniform distribution on [0,1]. Proposition B.2 can be viewed as an extension of the Skorohod representation theorem.
Now, we briefly explain the construction of the push-forward maps. An example is provided in B.1 to illustrate the construction. The NN architecture consists of three parts (see 1). The input dimension is the same as the number of connected components of the support NC​. For each component Ci​, let Hi​∈H([0,1]diC​,Ci​)∩FL​([0,1]diC​,Ci​), where diC​ is the dimension of component Ci​ in Assumption 3.4. By P=(Hi​)#​(Hi−1​)#​P on Ci​, we can approximate (Hi−1​)#​P first, which is supported on a unit cube. [43] constructs a wide NN g^​ of width W and constant depth such that W(g^​#​λ,(Hi​)#−1​P)⩽O(W−1/diC​) where λ is the uniform measure on [0,1]. Then, we approximate the Lipschitz map Hi​ to Ci​ to pull the distribution back to Ci​. These are the first two parts (yellow and blue blocks in 1) of the architecture.
Suppose that the output of i-th coordinate in the first two parts is vi​, the Gumbel-softmax layer in the third part (green box) combines different components of the support. In particular, we want to output vi​ with probability pi​=P(Ci​). Let V=[v1​,⋯,vi​], this can be achieved by outputting VX, where X=(X1​,⋯,XNC​​)T is a one-hot random vector with P(Xi​=1)=pi​. To use backpropagation in training, we use the Gumbel-Softmax trick [31] to (approximately) simulate such a random vector, X^iτ​=∑k=1NC​​exp((logpk​+Gk​)/τ)exp((logpi​+Gi​)/τ)​, where τ>0 is the temperature parameter (a hyperparameter) and Gi​∼Gumbel(0,1) are i.i.d. standard Gumbel variables. As τ→0, the distribution of X^τ converges almost surely to the categorical distribution [36, Proposition 1]. In particular, when τ=0, we denote X^i0​=Ii=argmaxj​{logpi​+Gi​}​. The output of the last layer is VX^τ. Note that the Gumbel-softmax function is differentiable with respect to parameter {log(pi​)}i=1,⋯,NC​​. Therefore, we can train the network with common gradient-based algorithms.
In summary, our construction has the form g^​=g^​3τ​∘g^​2​∘g^​1​, where g^​i​,i=1,2 have the separable form (g^​i1​(x1​),⋯,g^​iNC​​(xNC​​)) and g^​1j​∈NN1,djC​​(W1​,L1​),  g^​2j​∈NNdjC​,d​(W2​,L2​), j∈[NC​]; {djC​} are the dimension of cubes in Assumption 3.4. g^​3τ​ is the Gumbel-Softmax layer with temperature parameter τ>0. We slightly abuse the notations and denote this class of neural nets by NN(W1​,L1​,W2​,L2​,τ). Putting things together, we obtain the following theorem.

4 Consistency of Neural Causal Partial Identification

In this section, we prove the consistency of the max/min optimization approach to partial identification. In the finite sample setting, we consider the following estimator Fn​ of the optimal values of (1.1).
Fn​=M^∈NCMG​(F0,n​,F1,n​)argmin​s.t.   ​Et∼μT​​EM^​[F(V1​(t),⋯,VnV​​(t))],Sλn​​(Pmn​M^​(V),PnM∗​(V))⩽αn​,​(4.1)​
where PnM∗​,Pmn​M^​ are the empirical distribution of PM∗,PM^ with sample size n,mn​, μT​ is a given measure, Sλ​(⋅,⋅) is the Sinkhorn distance and Fi,n​ will be specified later. For example, the counterfactual outcome E[Y(1)] is a special case of the objective. Our results can be easily generalized to any linear combination of objective functions of this form. We use the Sinkhorn distance because it can be computed efficiently in practice [15]. We want to study if Fn​ is a good lower bound as n→∞. To match the observational distribution, we need to increase the width or depth of the NNs we use. As the sample size increases, the number of parameters also increases to infinity, which creates difficulty for our analysis. To obtain consistency, we need to regularize the functions while preserving their approximation power. Surprisingly, if we do not use any regularization, the following proposition implies that consistency may not hold even if the SCM is identifiable.

5 Experiments

In this section, we examine the performance of our algorithm in two settings. We compare our algorithm with the Autobounds algorithm [14] in a binary IV example in [14] and in a continuous IV model to calculate bounds for ATE 1The code can be found in https://github.com/Jiyuan-Tan/NeuralPartialID. Since Autobounds can only deal with discrete models, we discretize the continuous model for comparison purposes. The implementation details are provided in the D. We also provide an extra experiment on the counterexample of Proposition C.1 in the appendix to show the effect of Lipschitz regularization.

5.1 Discrete IV

The setting of the first experiment is taken from [14, Section D.1]. This is a binary IV problem and we can calculate the optimal bound using LP [4]. The causal graph is shown in 3. We find that our bound is close to the optimal bound. Both algorithms cover the true value in all runs. We could see from 1 that the bound given by NCM is slightly worse than Autobounds, but is still close to the optimal bound. Besides, the avgerage Autobounds bound does not cover the optimal bound in this example.

5.2 Continuous IV

Now, we turn to the continuous IV setting, where T is still binary, but Y and Z can be continuous. Let Eiλ​∼λZ1​+(1−λ)Unif(−1,1), where Z1​ is the Gaussian variable conditioning on [−1,1] and the structure equations of Mλ to be

where Eiλ​ are independent. It is easy to see the ATE of this model is 3 regardless of λ. In the experiment, we randomly choose ten λ∼Unif(0,1). For each λ, we run the algorithms 5 times to get the bound. We choose different latent distributions (indexed by λ) in the experiments to create more difficulty.
Since Autobounds can only deal with discrete variables, we discretize Z and Y. Suppose that Z∈[l,u], we map all points in intervals [l+i(u−l)/k,l+(i+1)(u−l)/k],I=0,1⋯,k−1 to the middle point l+(i+1/2)(u−l)/k. We choose k=8 in the following experiments. The choice will give rise to polynomial programming problems with 214 decision variables, which is quite large. 2 demonstrates the results. While both algorithms cover the true ATE well, we can see that NCM gives much tighter bounds on average. The main reason may be that the discretized problem does not approximate the original problem well enough. It is possible that a larger discretized parameter k can give a better bound, but since the size of the polynomial problem grows exponentially with k, the optimization problem may be intractable for large k. On the contrary, NCM does not suffer from computational difficulties.

6 Conclusion

In this paper, we provide theoretical justification for using NCMs for partial identification. We show that NCMs can be used to represent SCMs with complex unknown latent distributions under mild assumptions and prove the asymptotic consistency of the max/min estimator for partial identification of causal effects in general settings with both discrete and continuous variables. Our results also provide guidelines on the practical implementation of this method and on what hyperparameters are important, as well as recommendations on values that these hyperparameters should take for the consistency of the method. These practical guidelines were validated with a small set of targeted experiments, which also showcase superior performance of the neural-causal approach as compared to a prior main contender approach from econometrics and statistics, that involves discretization and polynomial programming.
An obvious next step in the theoretical foundation of neural-causal models is providing finite sample guarantees for this method, which requires substantial further theoretical developments in the understanding of the geometry of the optimization program that defines the bounds on the causal effect of interest. We take a first step in that direction for the special case, when there are no unobserved confounders and view the general case as an exciting avenue for future work.

Let λ be the Lebesgue measure on [0,1]. Given any probability measure P that satisfies Assumption 3.5, there exists a continuous curve γ:[0,1]→supp(P) such that γ#​λ=P. Furthermore, if d⩾1, γ is 1/d-Hölder continuous.
Before we prove Proposition B.2, we need to introduce some important notions. Let {Cn​} be a sequence of partitions of the unit cube [0,1]d. We say {Cn​} has property (*) if the following properties are satisfied.

The following lemma is important in the construction of the Hilbert curve.
Lemma B.3 (Algorithm 3 in [25]).
Original Given a sequence of partitions of the unit cube {Cn​} that has property (*), there exist a ordering for each partition Cn​, i.e.,
On​:{1,⋯,2nd}→{i1​i2​⋯in​​:ij​=0,⋯,2d−1},

D Experiments

The structure equations of the generative models are (3.3). We use three-layer feed-forward neural networks with width 128 for each f^​i​ and six-layer neural networks with width 128 for each g^​j​. We use the Augmented Lagrangian Multiplier (ALM) method to solve the optimization problems as in [3]. We run 600 epochs and use a batch size of 2048 in each epoch. mn​ is set to be mn​=n. The "geomloss" package [16] is used to calculate the Sinkhorn distance. To impose Lipschitz regularization, we use the technique from [23] to do layer-wise normalization to the weight matrices with respect to infinity norm. The upper bound of the Lipschitz constant in each layer is set to be 8. The τ in the Gumbel-softmax layer is set to be 0.
For the choice of Wasserstein ball radius αn​, we use the subsampling technique from [11, Section 3.4]. We can take the criterion function in [11] to be Q(θ)=W(PM∗(V),PMθ(V)) and its empirical estimation to be Qn​(θ)=W(PnM∗​(V),PnMθ​(V)). In the first step, we minimize the Wasserstein distance θ^n∗​=argminθ​W(PnM∗​(V),PnMθ​(V)). Then, [11] propose to refine the radius Qn​(θ^n∗​) by taking the quantile of subsample {supθ:Qn​(θ^)⩽βQn​(θ^n∗​)​Qj,b​(θ)}, where Qj,b​ denotes the criterion function estimated at j-th subsample of size b. However, it is time-consuming to solve this optimization problem many times. In practice, we set the radius αn​ to be the 95% quantile of {W(PˉjM∗​}(V),PnMθ^n∗​​(V)), where we use 50 subsamples PˉjM∗​,j=1,⋯,50 from PMn∗​(V) with size b=⌊15n​⌋.

We test our neural causal method on the counterexample in C.1. We choose the noise Uy​ to be the normal variable. The structure equations are
P(U1​=1)=3/5,P(U1​=0)=2/5XP(T=1∣X=x)Y​,P(U2​=1)=1/3,P(U1​=0)=2/3,={−10​,w.p. 1/2,,w.p. 1/2,​ ={1/25/8​,x=−1,,x=0,​ =⎩⎨⎧​T+Uy​U1​+Uy​U2​+Uy​​,X=−1,,X=0,T=1,,X=0,T=0,​​
We compare the confidence intervals of the unregularized neural casual method and the Lipschitz regularized one under different architectures. We choose the layerwise Lispchitz constants upper bound to be 5 and 1.2. As a benchmark, we also include the bound obtained by the Double Machine Learning estimator using the EconML package. The result is shown in 9. For this identifiable case example, the double ML estimator produces better bounds for the ATE. The intervals given by regularized and unregularized NCM are similar to the regularized one slightly better in the left figure, where we use medium-sized NNs. However, in the right figure, the obtained intervals after regularization are tighter, although slightly biased, compared with the regularized setting. From these two experiments, we conclude that the architecture of NNs will also influence the results and adding regularization during the training process can prevent extreme confidence intervals or inconsistency.

Let μ1​,⋯,μn​,μ^​1​,⋯,μ^​n​ be measure on Rd, for any p1​,⋯,pn​∈[0,1] such that ∑k=1n​pk​=1, we have
W(k=1∑n​pk​μk​,k=1∑n​pk​μ^​k​)⩽k=1∑n​pk​W(μk​,μ^​k​).
Proof.
For any 1-Lipschitz function f:Rd→R, we have
EX∼∑k=1n​pk​μk​​[f(X)]−EX∼∑k=1n​pk​μ^​k​​[f(X)]​=k=1∑n​pk​(EXk​∼μk​​[f(Xk​)]−EXk​∼μ^​k​​[f(Xk​)])⩽k=1∑n​pk​W(μk​,μ^​k​).​
By dual formulation of Wasserstein-1 distance,
W(k=1∑n​pk​μk​,k=1∑n​pk​μk​)​=f 1-Lipschitzsup​EX∼∑k=1n​pk​μk​​[f(X)]−EX∼∑k=1n​pk​μ^​k​​[f(X)]⩽k=1∑n​pk​W(μk​,μ^​k​).​

Lemma E.3.
Original Given two measures μ=μ1​⊗⋯⊗μn​,μ^​=μ^​1​⊗⋯⊗μ^​n​, we have
W(μ,μ^​)⩽k=1∑n​W(μk​,μ^​k​).
Clarified statement Given two measures μ=μ1​⊗⋯⊗μn​, μ^​=μ^​1​⊗⋯⊗μ^​n​, where every factor μk​ and μ^​k​ is a probability measure, we have
W(μ,μ^​)⩽k=1∑n​W(μk​,μ^​k​).
Proof.
Original step For any ϵ>0, let πk​ be a coupling of μk​,μ^​k​ such that
EXk​,Yk​∼πk​​[∥Xk​−Yk​∥1​]⩽W(μk​,μ^​k​)+ϵ.
Then,
W(μ,μ^​)​⩽Eπ1​⊗⋯⊗πn​​[∥X−Y∥]=k=1∑n​EXk​,Yk​∼πk​​[∥Xk​−Yk​∥1​]⩽W(μk​,μ^​k​)+ϵ.​

Corrected step If n=0, both empty products are the probability measure on the one-point space and both sides are zero.Suppose n⩾1.If any W(μk​,μ^​k​)=∞, the inequality holds in the extended nonnegative reals.Otherwise, for any ϵ>0 and every k∈[n], choose a probability coupling πk​ of μk​ and μ^​k​ such that
E(Xk​,Yk​)∼πk​​[∥Xk​−Yk​∥1​]⩽W(μk​,μ^​k​)+ϵ.

W(μ,μ^​)​⩽Eπ1​⊗⋯⊗πn​​[∥X−Y∥]=k=1∑n​E(Xk​,Yk​)∼πk​​[∥Xk​−Yk​∥1​]⩽k=1∑n​W(μk​,μ^​k​)+nϵ.​

∎
Lemma E.4 (Approximation error of Gumbel-Softmax layer).

Without loss of generality, we may assume that ∑k=1n​pk​=1. Otherwise, we can divide the denominator and numerator in (E.5) by ∑k=1n​pk​. Let Δn​={(x1​,⋯,xn​):∑k=1n​xk​=1}. We construct a transportation map T:Δn​→Δn​ as follows. T(x1​,⋯,xn​) is a n-dimensional vector with all zeros except that the i=argmaxj​xj​-th entry being one. If there are multiple coordinates that is maximum, we choose the first coordinate and let the remaining coordinate be zero. It is easy to verify that T#​μτ and μ0 have the same distribution [36]. For any δ>0, we have
P(∣Gk1​​+logpk1​​−(Gk2​​+logpk2​​)∣<δ)​=∫−∞∞​∫y+logpk1​​pk2​​−δy+logpk1​​pk2​​+δ​exp(−x−y−exp(−y)−exp(−x))dxdy⩽2δe−1∫−∞∞​exp(−y−exp(−y))dy=2δ,​
where we have used exp(−x−exp(−x))⩽exp(−1). Let event Eδ​={∃i,j∈[n]:∣Gi​+logpi​−(Gj​+logpj​)∣<δ}, we have
P(Eδ​)​⩽i=j∑​P(∣Gi​+logpi​−(Gj​+logpj​)∣<δ)⩽δn(n−1)e−1.​

EXτ∼μτ​[∥T(Xτ)−Xτ∥1​]​⩽P(Eδ​)EXτ∼μτ​[∥T(Xτ)−Xτ∥1​∣Eδ​]+P(Eδc​)EXτ∼μτ​[∥T(Xτ)−Xτ∥1​∣Eδc​].​
Note that ∥T(Xτ)−Xτ∥1​⩽2. For the first term, we have
P(Eδ​)EXτ∼μτ​[∥T(Xτ)−Xτ∥1​∣Eδ​]⩽2δn(n−1)e−1.
For the second term, under event Eδc​, let kmax​=argmaxi​Xi​, if j=kmax​=argmaxi​(logpk​+Gk​)
​∑k=1n​exp((logpk​+Gk​)/τ)exp((logpj​+Gj​)/τ)​−1​​=​∑k=1n​exp((logpk​+Gk​)/τ)∑k=j​exp((logpk​+Gk​)/τ)​​⩽​exp((logpj​+Gj​)/τ)∑k=j​exp((logpk​+Gk​)/τ)​​=k=j∑​exp((logpk​+Gk​−(logpj​+Gj​))/τ)⩽(n−1)exp(−δ/τ).​

W(μτ,μ0)⩽EXτ∼μτ​[∥T(Xτ)−Xτ∥1​]⩽2δn(n−1)e−1+2(n−1)exp(−δ/τ).

∎

Original For any μ∈Δn​,ν∈Δm​ and λ>0, we have
0⩽W1,λ​(μ,ν)−W(μ,ν)​⩽(log(mn)+1)λ,​

Lemma E.6.
Original Given a measure μ on Rd and a real function class F with output dimension d, suppose that the pseudo-dimension of F is less than dF​<∞ and there exists K>0 such that ∣f(x)∣⩽K,∀f∈F,x∈Rd′, then with probability at least 1−exp(O(δ−dlog(δ−1)+dF​logϵ−1−nϵ2)),
f∈Fsup​W(f#​μ,f#​μn​)​⩽δ+ϵ​
for all δ,ϵ>0, where μn​ is the empirical distribution of μ.
Corrected
Given a probability measure μ on Rd′ and a class F of measurable functions f:Rd′→Rd, suppose that each scalar coordinate class Fj​={x↦fj​(x):f∈F}, j∈[d], has pseudo-dimension less than dF​<∞ and there exists K>0 such that ∥f(x)∥∞​⩽K for all f∈F and x∈Rd′.
Suppose in addition that there are a standard Borel space T and a jointly Borel map G:T×Rd′→[−K,K]d such that F={G(t,⋅):t∈T}.
There are positive constants C,c depending only on d,K such that, with probability at least
1−exp(C((1+δ−d)log(2+δ−1)+dF​log(2+ϵ−1))−cnϵ2),
f∈Fsup​W(f#​μ,f#​μn​)⩽δ+ϵ​
for all δ,ϵ>0, where μn​ is the empirical distribution of μ.
Proof.
Original step By the dual formulation of the Wasserstein distance,
f∈Fsup​W(f#​μ,f#​μn​)​=h∈F1​(Rd,Rd),h(0)=0sup​f∈Fsup​EX∼μn​​[h∘f(X)]−EX∼μ​[h∘f(X)].​
We define
N1​(ϵ,F,n)​=x1​,⋯,xn​sup​N(ϵ,{(f(x1​),⋯,f(xn​):f∈F)},∥⋅∥1​),​
where N(ϵ,S,∥⋅∥1​) is the covering number of set S in ℓ1​ norm.
Corrected step The empty class satisfies the uniform assertion vacuously, so assume T=∅.Let X1​,…,Xn​ be independent observations with law μ.By the dual formulation of Wasserstein distance,
f∈Fsup​W(f#​μ,f#​μn​)=h∈Hsup​f∈Fsup​(EX∼μn​​h(f(X))−EX∼μ​h(f(X))),​
where
H={h:[−K,K]d→R:h(0)=0, ∣h(x)−h(y)∣⩽∥x−y∥}.
Every such h takes values in [−dK,dK].Retain the unnormalized empirical covering number
N1​(r,F,N)=x1​,…,xN​sup​N(r,{(f(x1​),…,f(xN​)):f∈F},∥⋅∥1​),​
where the 1-norm on the evaluation vector sums over all sample points and output coordinates.
With the uniform norm, H is closed, uniformly bounded and equicontinuous on the compact cube, hence is a compact metric space by Arzela–Ascoli.Evaluation (h,y)↦h(y) is continuous: its increment is bounded by ∥h−h′∥∞​+∥y−y′∥.Consequently (t,h,x)↦h(G(t,x)) is jointly Borel on T×H×Rd′.Its bounded population integral is Borel in (t,h): this holds for indicators of measurable rectangles, is preserved by bounded monotone limits and linear combinations, and extends to bounded Borel functions by the monotone class theorem.Every strict deviation event is the projection of a Borel set from this standard Borel parameter space and is therefore analytic and universally measurable; weak supremum events are countable intersections of strict ones.The same reasoning applies to two samples and finite coordinate swaps.All probabilities below are thus defined in the completion of the sample law.
Obviously, if h is 1-Lipschitz,
N1​(ϵ,h∘F,n)​⩽N1​(ϵ,F,n).​
Original step By Theorem 18.4 in [2], for any fixed h,
N1​(ϵ,h∘F,n)⩽N1​(ϵ,F,n)​⩽e(dF​+1)(ϵ2e​)dF​.​
By Theorem 17.1 in [2],
P(f∈Fsup​EX∼μn​​[h∘f(X)]−EX∼μ​[h∘f(X)]>ϵ)​⩽exp(O(dF​logϵ−1−nϵ2)).​
Let Hδ​ be the δ-net of the set H={h:h∈F1​([−K,K]d,[−K,K]d),h(0)=0}in ℓ∞​ norm. By Lemma 6 in [21],
∣Hδ​∣​⩽exp(O(δ−dlogδ−1)).​
Therefore, with probability no more than exp(O(δ−dlogδ−1+dF​logϵ−1−nϵ2))
h∈Hδ​,f∈Fsup​EX∼μn​​[h∘f(X)]−EX∼μ​[h∘f(X)]>ϵ.​
Notice that
h∈H,f∈Fsup​EX∼μn​​[h∘f(X)]−EX∼μ​[h∘f(X)]​⩽2δ+h∈Hδ​,f∈Fsup​EX∼μn​​[h∘f(X)]−EX∼μ​[h∘f(X)],​
which implies that with probability no more than exp(O(δ−dlogδ−1+dF​logϵ−1−nϵ2))
h∈H,f∈Fsup​EX∼μn​​[h∘f(X)]−EX∼μ​[h∘f(X)]>2δ+ϵ.​
Corrected step Put v=⌊dF​⌋.Each coordinate class has pseudo-dimension at most v.Normalize its range by fj​↦(fj​+K)/(2K).Applying Theorem 18.4 of [2] in its averaged empirical metric, and then undoing the normalization, bounds a scalar unnormalized cover of radius r/(2d) on N points by
e(v+1)(2+r8eKdN​)v.
The additional 2 allows radii beyond the normalized unit range.Take the product of these d covers.For every product ball meeting the evaluation vectors of F, choose one such vector as its center.Two vectors in that product ball differ by at most r/d in each scalar unnormalized metric, hence by at most r in the summed vector metric.Thus
N1​(r,F,N)⩽[e(v+1)(2+r8eKdN​)v]d.
This exhibits both sample-size and range scaling.
Fix h∈H, and define
af​(x)=2dKh(f(x))+dK​,zf​(x)=af​(x)​.
Both functions take values in [0,1].On N points, the inequality ∣a​−b​∣⩽∣a−b∣​ and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality give
N1​i=1∑N​∣zf​(xi​)−zg​(xi​)∣⩽(2dKN1​i=1∑N​∥f(xi​)−g(xi​)∥)1/2.
Consequently an unnormalized vector cover of radius 2dKNr2 gives an averaged scalar cover of the class {zf​:f∈F} of radius r, whose cardinality is at most
[e(v+1)(2+4e/r2)v]d.
By Theorem 17.1 in [2], with its standing measurability condition, let X and T0​ be standard Borel spaces, let g:T0​×X→[0,1] be jointly Borel, and put G={g(t,⋅):t∈T0​}=∅.For every Borel probability distribution P on X×[0,1], every 0<ζ<1 and every positive integer m,
Pm{some t∈T0​ has ​E(x,y)∼P​(g(t,x)−y)2−m1​i=1∑m​(g(t,xi​)−yi​)2​⩾ζ}⩽4N1avg​(ζ/16,G,2m)exp(−ζ2m/32).
Here the draws are independent, the probability is taken in the completed sample law, and N1avg​ uses the averaged empirical metric.For the present class, (t,x)↦(h(G(t,x))+dK)/(2dK)​ is jointly Borel, since h is continuous and the square root is continuous on [0,1].Its parameter space is the same standard Borel space T, and its constant-response input law is μ⊗δ0​.Apply this form of Theorem 17.1 to the class with response identically zero.Its squared loss is zf2​=af​.For 0<ϵ<2dK, put η=ϵ/(2dK) and use the averaged cover at radius η/16 on 2n points.The theorem gives
P(f∈Fsup​∣(μn​−μ)(h∘f)∣>ϵ)⩽4[e(v+1)(2+1024e/η2)v]dexp(−nη2/32).
Since v⩽dF​ and log(v+1)⩽v, the logarithm of the right-hand side is bounded by C0​+C1​dF​log(2+ϵ−1)−c1​nϵ2, with constants depending only on d,K.If ϵ⩾2dK, the deviation is deterministically at most 2dK, and the desired deviation bound is immediate.Let Hδ​ be a finite δ/2-net of H in the uniform norm.Such a net has
log∣Hδ​∣⩽C2​(1+δ−d)log(2+δ−1),
where C2​ depends only on d,K.To see this, take a grid in [−K,K]d with 1-norm mesh at most δ/8 and at most (1+C3​/δ)d points.Quantize the values of h at these points into bins of width at most δ/8 in [−dK,dK].There are at most 2+C4​/δ bins at each point.Choose one member of H from each nonempty quantization pattern.Two functions with the same pattern differ by at most δ/8 at grid points and by at most 3δ/8 everywhere, using their Lipschitz bounds and a nearest grid point.These representatives form the required net.Counting patterns gives the displayed entropy bound.Apply the fixed-h concentration bound to every h∈Hδ​ and take a union bound.For 0<ϵ<2dK, after enlarging a constant depending only on d,K,
P(h∈Hδ​,f∈Fsup​(μn​−μ)(h∘f)>ϵ)⩽exp(C((1+δ−d)log(2+δ−1)+dF​log(2+ϵ−1))−cnϵ2).
For every h∈H, choose h~∈Hδ​ with ∥h−h~∥∞​⩽δ/2.Since μn​ and μ are probability measures,
∣(μn​−μ)((h−h~)∘f)∣⩽δ.
Therefore
h∈H,f∈Fsup​(μn​−μ)(h∘f)⩽δ+h~∈Hδ​,f∈Fsup​(μn​−μ)(h~∘f).
The dual formula yields the stated Wasserstein bound.If ϵ⩾2dK, both push-forward measures are supported in a set of 1-norm diameter 2dK, so their Wasserstein distance is at most 2dK⩽δ+ϵ deterministically.This completes the proof for all positive δ,ϵ.
∎
Clarified statement By Theorem 18.4 in [2], if G is a nonempty class of functions from a set X into [0,1] with finite pseudo-dimension v, then for every 0<ϵ⩽1 and every positive integer m,
N1avg​(ϵ,G,m)⩽M1avg​(ϵ,G,m)<e(v+1)(ϵ2e​)v,​
where N1avg​(ϵ,G,m) and M1avg​(ϵ,G,m) are the largest, over x1​,…,xm​∈X, covering and packing numbers of {(g(x1​),…,g(xm​)):g∈G} in the averaged metric d1​(u,w)=m1​∑i=1m​∣ui​−wi​∣.
This is Theorem 18.4 in [2].
Clarified statement
The cited assertion used in Lemma E.6 is the following restricted form of Theorem 17.1 in [2], with its standing measurability condition.
Let X and T be standard Borel spaces, let g:T×X→[0,1] be jointly Borel, and put G={g(t,⋅):t∈T}=∅.
For every Borel probability distribution P on X×[0,1], every 0<ϵ<1 and every positive integer m,
​Pm{some t∈T has ​E(x,y)∼P​(g(t,x)−y)2−m1​i=1∑m​(g(t,xi​)−yi​)2​⩾ϵ}⩽4N1avg​(ϵ/16,G,2m)exp(−ϵ2m/32).​
Here the sample consists of independent draws from P, the probability is taken in its completion, and N1avg​(r,G,N) is the supremum over x1​,…,xN​∈X of the covering number of the evaluation vectors in the metric N−1∑i​∣ui​−vi​∣.
This structural domain supplies the standing measurability condition: the loss is bounded and jointly Borel, and its integral against P is Borel in t.
The latter assertion holds for indicators of measurable rectangles, is preserved by bounded monotone limits and linear combinations, and hence holds for bounded Borel functions by the monotone class theorem.
Each bad event is a projection of a Borel subset of T×(X×[0,1])m, so it is analytic and universally measurable.
Replacing the sample by two independent samples or applying any of the finitely many coordinate swaps gives Borel functions on finite products and therefore the same measurability conclusion.
Thus the sample and ghost-sample events used by Theorem 17.1 are measurable in the completed sample laws, and that theorem gives the displayed inequality.

comments.excerpt: \vsLine\textbf{Claim:} A Neural Causal Model has i.i.d. multivariate uniform latent inputs and neural structural functions. \vsLine\textbf{What is wrong:} \vsSu
comments.label: TheoremChecker
comments.html: Claim: A Neural Causal Model has i.i.d. multivariate uniform latent inputs and neural structural functions. What is wrong: “… all Ui​ are i.i.d. multivariate uniform variables, GVi​​ are i.i.d Gumblel variables and functions in (2.1) are Neural Networks (NNs).” The phrase “i.i.d. multivariate uniform variables” admits either identical block laws of one common dimension or independent unit-cube blocks of their indicated dimensions. Counterexample: Let Z1​,Z2​,Z3​ be independent Unif([0,1]) variables. Set U1​=(Z1​) and U2​=(Z2​,Z3​), and take independent standard Gumbel coordinates independent of these variables. The coordinate convention gives independent uniform blocks on [0,1] and [0,1]2, whereas the common-block-dimension reading requires padding before calling the two block laws identical. Proposed fix: Specify i.i.d. scalar uniform coordinates grouped into blocks of their indicated dimensions, retain independence of every Gumbel coordinate and the neural structural and propensity-weight requirements, and use ignored coordinates if padding is desired. This protects the product law and every architecture and approximation conclusion of Corollary 3.7.

comments.label: TheoremChecker

Claim: Theorem 3.3 bounds every interventional Wasserstein error by a constant depending only on L,K,G times the structural uniform infinity errors and latent Wasserstein error. What is wrong: (a) “… we have
∫g(u,t,v1​,⋯,vk​) d(μVk​∣U0​,T,1:k−1T​−μ^​V^k​∣U^0​,T,1:k−1T​)=g(u,t,v1​,⋯,vk−1​,fk​(pa(vk​),uVk​​))−g(u,t,v1​,⋯,vk−1​,f^​k​(pa(vk​),uVk​​))⩽​fk​(pa(vk​),uVk​​)−f^​k​(pa(vk​),uVk​​)​∞​⩽S,​
where we have used the Lipschitz property of g in the first inequality.” A 1-Lipschitz scalar test function controls the structural output 1-norm, which can be dk​ times its coordinatewise infinity norm. (b) “We have
k=1∑ni​​∫pk​g(u,t,x1​,⋯,k) d(μU0​,T,1:k−1T​−μ^​U0​,T,1:k−1T​)⩽LW(μU0​,T,1:k−1T​,μ^​U^0​,T,1:k−1T​).”
The conditional probabilities vary with the history being integrated, so the kernel difference contains a probability-variation term omitted from the displayed Lipschitz bound. Counterexample: Take two isolated roots T and V1​∈R100, with independent UT​,U1​∼Unif([−1,1]). Set T=UT​, f1​(u)=(u/100,…,u/100), and f^​1​(u)=f1​(u)+(1/100,…,1/100), keeping the latent laws unchanged. Take L=K=1 and intervene at T=0. Then S=1/100 and the latent Wasserstein error is zero, whereas the interventional output Wasserstein error is 1; the proof's coefficient 4 gives the false inequality 1⩽4/100, and arbitrary output dimension rules out any coefficient uniform in that dimension. Proposed fix: The suggested version permits dimension and cardinality dependence in the comparison constant, inserts the missing norm factors, and includes the probability-variation term in the categorical kernel bound. Its fixed-dimension estimate protects the full approximation and convergence rates of Corollary 3.7, Theorem 4.2, and Corollary 4.4. Gives up: Uniformity of the comparison constant over unbounded continuous output dimensions and categorical cardinalities at fixed L,K and abstract causal graph. (This fix weakens the result.)

comments.excerpt: \vsLine\textbf{Claim:} Theorem~\ref{thm:wide_nn} asserts wide and deep neural distribution approximation rates for every mixed support allowed by Assumption~\re
comments.label: TheoremChecker
comments.html:
Claim: Theorem 3.6 asserts wide and deep neural distribution approximation rates for every mixed support allowed by Assumption 3.4. What is wrong: (a) “There exists a neural network g^​∈NN(W1​,Θ(maxj​djC​),Θ(d⋅maxj​djC​),L2​,τ) with the above architecture (1) such that
W(g^​#​λ,P)⩽O(W1−1/maxi​{diC​}​+L2−2/maxi​{diC​}​+(τ−τlogτ)).”
The citation application leaves the local refinement integer n either fixed or increasing with W1​, which gives different quantization requirements and does not determine the asserted width-dependent approximation. (b) In the clause quoted in (a): For n⩾2, the choice 1/⌈n(n−1)⌉ is neither an admissible δ nor an admissible mesh δ/n under the source's requirement δ<1/(n(n−1)), and it is not the source's positive integer depth parameter s. (c) The clause quoted in (a) uses Theorem 2 of [52], which the paper assumes only for scalar approximation on a cube with positive input dimension, but applies it to a support component with diC​=0. (d) “… there exists a neural network g^​∈NN(Θ(maxj​djC​),L1​,Θ(d⋅maxj​djC​),L2​,τ) with the above architecture such that
W(g^​#​λ,P)⩽O(L1−2/maxi​{diC​}​+L2−2/maxi​{diC​}​+(τ−τlogτ)).”
When every component is a singleton, the displayed exponent divides by maxi​diC​=0 and the displayed architecture budgets use this zero maximum. Counterexample: Let P=21​Unif([0,1]2)+21​δ(3,3)​ on R2. Take C1​=[0,1]2, C2​={(3,3)}, d1C​=2, and d2C​=0, with the identity chart on C1​ and the unique chart on C2​. At refinement n=2, the printed fraction equals 1/2. These support hypotheses hold, but interpreting the fraction as δ gives δ=1/2, interpreting it as δ/n gives δ=1, and both violate δ<1/2; the coordinate approximation on C2​ also invokes the undefined rate L2−2/0​. Proposed fix: Keep the approximation rates, instantiate Theorem VIII.1 of [43] with s=1, n=⌊(W1​/Aq​)1/q⌋ for q=diC​⩾1, and δ=1/⌈q​(q+1)n(n−1)⌉, and derive the width and 1-norm error bounds explicitly. Use this same admissible choice in the citation's parameter specification. Construct singleton blocks exactly, use DC​=max{1,maxi​diC​}, and state the deep construction separately under its lower-bound assumption. Derive the absolute width factors 64DC​ and 64dDC​ for that deep construction by parallelization, clipping, signed-coordinate transport, and padding. These choices protect the full approximation strengths used by Corollary 3.7, Theorem 4.2, and Corollary 4.4.

comments.excerpt: \vsLine\textbf{Claim:} Corollary~\ref{corollary:deep_nn} asserts the displayed neural approximation rate uniformly over every intervention, including arbitrary
comments.label: TheoremChecker
comments.html:
Claim: Corollary 3.7 asserts the displayed neural approximation rate uniformly over every intervention, including arbitrary real values of continuous treatments. What is wrong: (a) “…
f^​i​=⎩⎨⎧​argminf^​i​∈NNdiin​,diout​​(diout​(2diin​+10),L0​)​∥f^​i​−fi​∥∞​,Vi​ continuous,max{0,argf^​i​∈NNdiin​,diout​​(diout​(2diin​+10),L0​)min​∥f^​i​−fi​∥∞​},Vi​ categorical.​​”
This step uses uniform approximation of the structural functions by the selected neural networks, which the paper assumes only for the bounded cubes on which the approximation errors are minimized, but applies it to structural inputs containing generated latent values, generated parent values, and arbitrary real intervention values. (b) “By [52, Theorem 2], we have, if Vi​ is continuous, ∥f^​i​−fi​∥∞​⩽O(L0−1/diin​​)⩽O(L0−1/dmaxin​​).” The stated exponent gives only O(L0−1/diin​​), whereas the final estimate requires O(L0−2/diin​​). (c) “… p=f(pa(vk​),uVk​​),p^​=f^​(pa(vk​),uVk​​)/∥f^​∥1​.” Truncation at zero permits the entire approximating propensity vector to vanish outside its approximation cube, making division by its 1-norm undefined. (d) “…
∥p−p^​∥∞​⩽∥f^​∥1​1​∥f^​(pa(vk​),uVk​​)−f(pa(vk​),uVk​​)∥∞​+∥f^​∥1​1​∣∥f^​∥1​−1∣∥f∥∞​⩽∥f^​∥1​(ni​+1)​S⩽1−ni​S(ni​+1)​S⩽2(K+1)S​
where we use Assumption 3.2 that ni​⩽K and S⩽1/(2K).” A bound on realized categorical values does not imply ni​⩽K when some categories have zero probability. (e) In the step quoted in (b): The displayed power divides by zero for diin​=0, and the final powers are undefined when a maximum input or latent dimension is zero. (f) “… djU​ is the dimension of latent variables Uj​ and L1​,L2​,τ are hyperparameters of the neural network defined in Theorem 3.6.” The architectural width orders admit either absolute multiplicative factors or factors depending on the fixed causal model and R. Counterexample: Let G consist of T→Y, with independent latent variables UT​,UY​∼Unif([0,1]). Set fT​(u)=u and fY​(t,u)=sint, so that T=UT​ and Y=sinT, and take L=K=1. Use the identity support chart for each latent law, with domination constant 1 and zero boundary mass. For t∈R, intervene at T=t, giving PM∗(Y(t))=δsint​. For any fixed finite neural causal model of the displayed architecture, write a(t)=E[Y^(t)]. For this same model, consider the family of structural width allowances W0​(R)=⌈R⌉dmaxin​dmaxout​ for R⩾1. The generated latent support is compact, so the finitely many affine regions of the structural ReLU network make a(t) affine for all sufficiently large t, implying supt∈R​W(PM∗(Y(t)),PM^(Y^(t)))⩾1, whereas the claimed uniform bound tends to zero. The allowances W0​(R) have the stated order for each fixed R under the model-dependent reading, but their multiplicative factors are unbounded as R→∞, distinguishing that reading from an absolute width factor. Proposed fix: For each fixed R>0, restrict continuous intervention coordinates to [−R,R], specify a cube containing every corresponding true structural input, extend the structural functions by interpolation and input projection, and choose neural approximants with layers reserved for projection and positive categorical floors. Use the source's exponent 2/diin​, normalize with constants depending on the fixed cardinalities, and handle zero input dimensions by exact constant networks while requiring positive maximum dimensions in the displayed rate. Taking R=K protects the approximation used by Theorem 4.2 and Corollary 4.4. Replace the obsolete latent-law reference by the proposition entitled “Deep distribution approximation”, retaining its support, componentwise domination, and pullback boundary-null conditions. Specify absolute width factors and derive the common numerical factor 64 by parallelization, clipping, signed-coordinate transport, and padding, preserving the full architecture assertion. Gives up: A single neural model with the displayed error bound uniformly over unbounded continuous treatment values, and the displayed-rate statement when dmaxin​=0 or dmaxU​=0. (This fix weakens the result.)

comments.html:
Claim: Theorem 4.2 asserts almost-sure bounds [liminfn​Fn​,limsupn​Fn​]⊂[F​L^f​,F∗​] for the printed empirical optimizer and sampling radius. What is wrong: (a) “… Thus, P([−K,K]djU​) are compact and the space (M,d) is compact space. Closed set Θ∞​⊂M is also compact.” The raw-network Lipschitz restriction does not bound the Lipschitz constant of q/∥q∥1​, so the categorical parameter class is not equicontinuous and its limits need not satisfy the population bound L^f​. (b) “…
θ∈Θ∞​sup​∣gn​(θ)−g(θ)∣⩽O(log(nmn​)λn​+δn​+mn−1/(dmaxU​+2)​logmn​)=sn​,
where sn​ is defined in Theorem 4.2.” This step uses Lemma E.3, which the paper assumes only for comparison measures that are products of their coordinate measures, but applies it to the paired empirical law Pmn​θ​(U), which is not the product of its empirical marginals. (c) In the step quoted in (b): The empirical observation error includes categorical Gumbel fluctuations that are absent from the retained non-Gumbel latent marginal errors. (d) In the step quoted in (b): A positive-temperature Gumbel-softmax generator has a soft mixture output, rather than the displayed hard selected population mixture. (e) In the step quoted in (b): Even a hard selector has random empirical component counts, so its empirical law is not a mixture of component empirical laws with the unchanged population weights. (f) “Let
Θ∞​=∪n=1∞​Θn​​,gn​(θ)=Sλn​​(Pnθ∗​(V),Pmn​θ​(V)),f(θ)=Et∼μT​​EMθ​[F(V1​(t),⋯,VnV​​(t))]
and Θ~∞​={θ∗}.” Common-draw empirical laws depend on the generator representation, which is not determined by the latent population laws in θ, so the displayed definition does not determine gn​(θ). (g) In the step quoted in (b): The population comparison bound does not control the discrepancies between representation-dependent empirical laws in the population metric d. (h) The step quoted in (b) uses the current-depth pseudo-dimension bound and Lemma E.6, which the paper assumes only for the current fixed generator architecture, but applies it to Θ∞​, which contains the closures of arbitrarily deep future generator classes. (i) “…
FLK​={f:∥f∥∞​⩽K,f Lipschitz continuous}
and P(K) is the probability space on K.” The displayed definition of FLK​ requires each function to be Lipschitz but supplies no common Lipschitz bound, so functions x↦sin(rx) with arbitrarily large r belong to it when K=1. (j) “Take the Wasserstein radius to be αn​=O(sn​+ϵn​), Proposition C.2 implies the conclusion.” The coordinatewise output bound used for compactness permits f(x)=(K,K), which violates the uniform output 1-norm bound supx​∥f(x)∥1​⩽K in (4.2), so that compactness argument does not place every limit in its feasible class. (k) “… take the radius to be αn​=ϵn​+sn​,ϵn​=O(W0,n−1/dmaxin​​+∑i=12​Li,n−2/dmaxU​​+τn​logτn​),
sn​=O(mn−1/(dmaxU​+2)​logmn​+n−1/max{2,dmaxU​}log2(n)+log(nmn​)λn​).”
The reciprocal-dimensional exponents are undefined when dmaxin​=0 or dmaxU​=0. (l) “… we have verified the third assumption in Proposition C.2.” The coordinatewise bound in Assumption 3.2 permits a continuous structural output (K,K), whereas a uniform approximating sequence whose output 1-norm is at most K cannot converge to that output. (m) In the step quoted in (b): The uniform sampling argument does not verify the class measurability condition required by the concentration theorem for its neural and categorical selector families; individual measurability alone does not justify this invocation. Counterexample: Take the graph T→Y without bidirected edges, independent UT​,UY​∼Unif([−1,1]), and independent standard categorical Gumbel noises. Set T=UT​ and fY​(t,u)=(1−r(t),r(t)), where r(t)=1/2+∣t∣/8, with Y∈{1,2}, K=2, Lf​=1, F(T,Y)=Y, and μT​=δ0​. For 0<δ⩽1, let qδ​(t,u)=(δ(1/2−∣t∣/8),δ∣t∣/8+min{∣t∣,δ}/2) be the raw categorical network. Use exact affine generators for the latent laws, independent observational and common simulation samples, mn​=n, W0,n​=n, Li,n​=⌈n1/6⌉, and τn​=λn​=n−2, with positive tolerances and sufficiently large sampling-radius constants of the printed orders. For each finite common simulation sample, choose δn​>0 smaller than every simulated ∣T∣, which is possible almost surely. The true network is eventually feasible almost surely, and qδn​​/∥qδn​​∥1​ produces the identical simulated observations but objective value 1 under treatment zero, so Fn​=1 eventually, whereas F​2=F∗​=3/2. Proposed fix: Keep F​L^f​ and its uniform output 1-norm bound. Add supx​∥fi​(x)∥1​⩽K for each true continuous structural function and impose the same bound on continuous candidates. Restrict normalized categorical propensities to Lipschitz constant L^f​, assume dmaxin​,dmaxU​⩾1, use the joint-dimension sampling radius, specify the common Lipschitz bound in FLK​, and index empirical constraints by network representations on common exogenous draws. Verify locally that the restricted neural parameter sets are Borel, that categorical selections and finite-table ambiguity indicators have jointly Borel evaluation including ties and zero propensities, and that the normalized square-root tests preserve this property. The full generator parameter space supplies a measurable envelope with the same complexity bound. Analytic projections make the uniform events and empirical infimum measurable in the completed laws. These local verifications impose no further assumption on Theorem 4.2 and protect its almost-sure conclusion and the accepted O(αn​​) rate of Corollary 4.4. Gives up: The guarantee for the printed optimizer is replaced by a guarantee for candidates whose continuous structural functions have uniform output 1-norm at most K and whose normalized categorical propensities have Lipschitz constant at most L^f​. True models whose continuous structural functions violate that output 1-norm bound on the input domain are excluded, even when every output coordinate is bounded by K. The sampling orders based only on dmaxU​ and the rate for the original αn​ are given up. The displayed-order version excludes dmaxin​=0 and dmaxU​=0. (This fix weakens the result.)

Claim: Proposition 4.3 bounds the integrated squared difference of interventional outcome means by the displayed linear and quadratic Wasserstein terms under overlap, no confounding, and the structural Lipschitz and boundedness assumptions. What is wrong: (a) “Note that fy​(x,t)=EM​[Y∣X=x,T=t] is Ly​-Lipschitz continuous with Lipschitz constant Ly​⩽(L+1)nV​.” Lipschitz categorical propensity vectors can produce an outcome regression whose slope exceeds (L+1)nV​ because distances between categorical labels enter the outcome mean. (b) “This is because Y can be written as Y=F0​(X,T,Uy​) where Uy​ are latent variables independent of T,X and F0​ is composition of fi​ in structure equations.” An observed ancestor can affect both X=Pa(T) and Y, so its latent input to Y need not be independent of X even without hidden confounding. (c) “…
(∫fy​(x,t)ν(dx)−∫f^​y​(x,t)ν(dx))2⩾21​(∫fy​(x,t)ν(dx)−∫f^​y​(x,t)μ(dx))2            −(∫f^​y​(x,t)μ(dx)−∫f^​y​(x,t)ν(dx))2⩾21​(∫fy​(x,t)ν(dx)−∫f^​y​(x,t)μ(dx))2−Ly2​W2(μ,ν)=21​(EM​[Y(t)]−EM^​[Y^(t)])2−Ly2​W2(μ,ν).​”
The observational bound ∣Y^∣⩽K bounds its regression only almost surely under its observational input law and need not bound a structural regression version that represents intervention means at inputs outside that law's support. (d) “… we get
∫t1​t2​​(EM​[Y(t)]−EM^​[Y^(t)])2P(dt)⩽δ2CW​​W(μ,ν)+2Ly2​W2(μ,ν)(t2​−t1​).”
The quadratic coefficient obtained here is 2Ly2​, and the bound Ly​⩽(L+1)nV​ does not justify the statement's coefficient 2(L+1)nV​. (e) In the step quoted in (d): Integrating a constant against P(dt) on [t1​,t2​] gives its multiple by P([t1​,t2​]), whereas the displayed remainder uses t2​−t1​ and the nondescendant calculation switches to Lebesgue measure. Counterexample: Take the unconfounded continuous graph T→V2​→V3​→Y, with nV​=4, L=100, K=1, p=10−8, and η=10−9. Let U1​ have law P=(1−p)Unif([0,η])+pUnif([1−η,1]), and let the other three singleton canonical noises be independent uniform variables on [0,1], independent of U1​ and unused in the structural equations. Define ϕ(x)=min{max{100x,0},1}. In M, set T=U1​, V2​=ϕ(T), V3​=ϕ(V2​), and Y=ϕ(V3​). In M^, use the same latent law and set T^=min{U1​,η}, V^2​=100T^, V^3​=100V^2​, and Y^=100V^3​. Take t1​=0, t2​=1, and δ=1, so that T has law P and the conditional density relative to P is pν​(t)=1. Couple the models using their common latent variables, so their observed vectors agree on the first mixture component and each coordinate difference is at most 1 on the second component, giving W(μ,ν)⩽4p. All observational variables and non-Gumbel latents are bounded by 1 and all structural functions are at most 100-Lipschitz, but on [1−η,1] the intervention means are 1 and 106t, so the left-hand side is at least p(106(1−η)−1)2>9999, whereas the printed right-hand side is at most 8CW​p+32(1014)p2<50 with CW​=6(1014)=624362406. Proposed fix: Condition on all observed nondescendants of T and couple categorical transitions to obtain Ly​=(LD+1)nV​, where D=max({1}∪{(ni​−1)/2:Vi​ is categorical}). Derive the structural regression bound B=K(1+2qLy​) on the bounded input domain from an observational regression value and the Lipschitz inequality, where q is the numerical dimension of V, and replace the linear constant by CW​=4Ly​B+2Bmax{Ly​,1}. Retain the quadratic coefficient 2Ly2​ and integrate its remainder as P([t1​,t2​]). No additional hypothesis is needed; these constants protect the full O(αn​​) rate of Corollary 4.4 under its existing assumptions. Gives up: The linear coefficient based on a bound of K for structural regressions at every intervention input, the regression coefficient independent of categorical cardinalities, the unsquared quadratic coefficient 2(L+1)nV​, and interval-length scaling of the remainder for arbitrary probability measures P.

comments.html:
Claim: Corollary 4.4 asserts an O(αn​​) error for the uniform intervention objective under the assumptions of Proposition 4.3 and Theorem 4.2. What is wrong: (a) “We get that
W(PM∗(V),Pθn​(V))⩽W(PnM∗​(V),PM∗(V))+W(PM∗(V),Pθn​(V))+W(Pmn​θn​​(V),Pθn​(V))⩽O(αn​).”
The middle term repeats the population Wasserstein distance instead of the distance between the two empirical laws, so the displayed inequality does not establish the asserted upper bound. (b) “By Proposition 4.3, we get ∣Fn​−F∗​∣⩽O(αn​​).” Proposition 4.3 bounds the squared response difference integrated against P, whereas the objective integrates against μT​=Unif([t1​,t2​]), and the assumptions impose no relation between these measures. (c) “… (4.1) has feasible solutions and
W(PnM∗​(V),PM∗(V))⩽O(αn​),W(Pmn​θn​​(V),Pθn​(V))⩽O(αn​),
where notations θ and Pθ are defined in the proof of Theorem 4.2 and θn​ is one of the minimizers of (4.1).” The sampling assertion invokes uniform concentration without verifying its standing class measurability condition for the neural, normalized square-root and categorical indicator families used to establish feasibility and the uniform simulation estimate. Counterexample: Take the unconfounded graph T→Y and independent UT​,UY​∼Unif([0,1]). Let the true structural equations be T=UT​ and Y=UY​, and take K=2, Lf​=1, t1​=0, and t2​=2. Use the identity homeomorphism for each latent support, with Cf​=1, so both latent laws satisfy the support and lower-bound assumptions. Take P=Unif([0,1]) and the conditional density version pν​(t)=1 on [0,2], which represents the treatment law relative to P and satisfies overlap with δ=1. Take the candidate equations T^=U^T​ and Y^=max{−2,min{U^Y​−max{T^−1,0},2}}, with independent uniform latent laws generated by identity networks. Choose mn​=n, W0,n​=n, L1,n​,L2,n​=Θ(n1/6), τn​=n−1, and λn​=n−2, and take ϵn​=c1​n−1/3 and sn​=c2​n−1/3logn with sufficiently large fixed positive c1​,c2​, so that dmaxU​=1, dmaxin​=2, and the printed radius prescription holds with αn​=ϵn​+sn​=Θ(n−1/3logn). Let ρ=Unif([0,1]2) be the common observational law of the true and candidate models. Form the true and candidate empirical observational laws from independent samples of n independent complete observations with law ρ. Let xn​=Cn−1/2log2n for a fixed sufficiently large C>0. Let En​ be the event that both W(PnM∗​(V),ρ)⩽xn​ and W(PnM^​(V),ρ)⩽xn​. The bounded two-dimensional concentration inequality in Theorem 2 of [17] gives P(Enc​)⩽C0​exp(−c0​n(xn​/log(2+1/xn​))2)=O(n−3), and on En​ the triangle inequality and Lemma E.5 give Sλn​​(PnM∗​(V),PnM^​(V))⩽2xn​+2(1+2logn)n−2=o(n−1/3logn)⩽αn​ eventually, so the candidate is feasible with probability at least 1−O(n−2) while its uniform intervention objective is 1/2−21​∫12​(t−1)dt=1/4 and F∗​=1/2, whence Fn​⩽1/4 and ∣Fn​−F∗​∣⩾1/4 contradict the asserted rate as αn​→0; the response difference vanishes P-almost surely but is nonzero on (1,2]. Proposed fix: Assume t1​<t2​ and μT​≪P with a square-integrable Radon–Nikodym density, and use the continuous output 1-norm bound, normalized categorical restrictions, population structural classes and joint sampling radius of Theorem 4.2. Correct the empirical middle term and derive the uniform objective bound by Cauchy–Schwarz. Verify standard Borel neural parameterization and jointly Borel evaluation of the actual categorical indicators and their normalized square-root tests, using a measurable generator envelope with the same growth bound. Verify measurability of the empirical optimal value by analytic projection. These local proofs preserve the accepted estimator, assumptions and O(αn​​) rate of Corollary 4.4 without a further class measurability premise. comments.excerpt: \vsLine\textbf{Claim:} Lemma~\ref{lemma:sup_wasserstein} asserts a uniform empirical Wasserstein bound controlled by $d_{\mathcal F}$ and a bounded vector outpu
comments.label: TheoremChecker
comments.html:
Claim: Lemma E.6 asserts a uniform empirical Wasserstein bound controlled by dF​ and a bounded vector output range. What is wrong: (a) “…
P(f∈Fsup​EX∼μn​​[h∘f(X)]−EX∼μ​[h∘f(X)]>ϵ)⩽exp(O(dF​logϵ−1−nϵ2)).”
The scalar source theorem does not identify whether the vector pseudo-dimension means the maximum coordinate pseudo-dimension or the pseudo-dimension on the augmented domain of coordinate indices. (b) In the step quoted in (a): The displayed covering bound omits the factor of sample size required by the explicitly unnormalized empirical 1-norm. (c) The step quoted in (a) uses Theorem 18.4 of [2], which the paper assumes only for scalar functions with range [0,1] in the averaged empirical metric, but applies it to the unnormalized evaluation vectors of functions bounded by an arbitrary K. (d) In the step quoted in (a): The invocation of Theorem 17.1 of [2] omits its standing measurability condition on the function class, which does not follow from measurability of each function and finite pseudo-dimension. (e) The step quoted in (a) uses Theorem 17.1 of [2], which the paper assumes only for squared losses of [0,1]-valued functions with responses in [0,1], but applies it to the unnormalized scalar expectations of h∘f. Counterexample: Let d=d′=1, μ=Unif([−1,1]), K=1, and h(x)=x. Let F={fc​:c∈[0,1/2]}, where fc​(x)=c+21​I{x⩾0}​, and take dF​=2. Take n=10000 and ϵ=1/4. Evaluation vectors have distance n∣c−c′∣, so N1​(1/4,F,10000)⩾10000, whereas the attributed bound is 192e3<4000; increasing the range also violates that bound even in the averaged metric. Proposed fix: State the coordinatewise pseudo-dimension condition explicitly, retain the unnormalized covering definition with its sample-size and range scaling, and apply the squared-loss concentration theorem to the square root of a normalized scalar test function. Use scalar dual functions and a δ/2-net. State that F has a standard Borel parameter space with jointly Borel evaluation, and verify this property for the scalar dual and normalized square-root families. Take uniform-event probabilities in the completed sample law. This supplies the standing measurability condition without assuming a concentration inequality and preserves the sampling order required by Theorem 4.2 and Corollary 4.4.

texHtml.Take $d=2$ and let $\\mathcal{C}_n$ be t: Take d=2 and let Cn​ be the rectangular grid with 4⌈n/2⌉ columns and 4⌊n/2⌋ rows, including cell boundaries. Every cell has four children, so property (*) holds. The first three grids have sizes 4×1, 4×4, and 16×4. At the first level, adjacency forces the four columns to be visited consecutively. At the second level, the four horizontal cells within each column must be visited vertically, in one of the two directions. At the third level, each such cell has four vertical-strip children, whose ordering must run horizontally from one extreme strip to the other. Across successive vertically adjacent second-level cells, these horizontal directions must alternate. Consequently, after four such cells, the first and last third-level cells within a first-level column lie on the same horizontal extreme. An interior first-level column must instead enter from one neighboring column and exit toward the other, requiring opposite extremes. This contradiction rules out the asserted orderings.
